title: AR Rahman Pitches Kashmir as Global Cinema Hub, Urges Bollywood to Film There
excerpt: The Oscar-winning composer told ANI in Srinagar that Bollywood should project Kashmir's beauty and peace rather than its troubled past, praising the International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir as a launchpad for global recognition.
body:
• Oscar-winning composer AR Rahman has urged Bollywood to film more in Kashmir, calling the Valley “beautiful” and “blessed” in an interview with ANI in Srinagar on September 12.
  • Rahman said Bollywood should project Kashmir’s beauty and peace rather than dwelling on violence and the past: “The past is past, and the future is bright.”
  • He praised the International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir as a commendable initiative that could put the Valley on the global cultural map.
  • The composer also revealed plans for future collaborations in Kashmir, including a possible live performance, and recalled recording Kashmiri folk singers for “Rockstar.”

Oscar-winning music composer AR Rahman has called on Bollywood to shoot more films in Kashmir, pitching the Valley as an ideal global hub for cinema in an interview with news agency ANI in Srinagar on Friday.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=iJoXjSddkxY

“Kashmir is a beautiful place and it’s blessed,” Rahman said. “Having an international film festival is commendable, and everybody can see the beauty of Kashmir and the vibration of Kashmir. I wish this film festival becomes really famous and a lot of people come here and enjoy the hospitality of the Kashmiri people.”

A pitch for the Valley on the world stage

Rahman welcomed the International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir, saying the initiative could showcase the Valley’s scenic beauty, vibrant culture, and warm hospitality to the world. He said Kashmir’s peaceful surroundings and natural beauty make it an ideal destination for filmmakers and artists seeking inspiration, and expressed hope the festival gains global recognition.

https://x.com/CM_JnK/status/2098437295175237915

Asked whether Bollywood should increasingly use Kashmir as a filming destination, Rahman was direct. “That’s a very good point. I think that’s what should happen from now,” he said. “They should bring the beauty and the peace when you see nature as a positive thing rather than talking about violence or the past.”

“They should bring the beauty and the peace when you see nature as a positive thing rather than talking about violence or the past. The past is past, and the future is bright.”

— AR Rahman

Rockstar roots and a return

The composer has a personal history with the Valley: he recorded Kashmiri women singing folk songs for his score to Imtiaz Ali’s “Rockstar” (2011). “I came here for ‘Rockstar,’” he recalled. “I recorded the ladies singing folk songs, and we used it in Rockstar. We want to come and do more things here.”

Rahman said he is exploring further collaborations in Kashmir, including with local musicians, and revealed that discussions are underway for a possible live performance. “Yes, we have some plans, and we are talking. Hopefully, I want to come and perform here,” he said. The composer is currently in Kashmir for an advertising shoot, which he said had just been completed.

Why it matters

Rahman’s endorsement carries unusual weight. As one of the few Indian artists with genuine global name recognition — his two Academy Awards for “Slumdog Millionaire” made him a household name far beyond the diaspora — his pitch effectively markets Kashmir to the world’s film industries. For the Valley’s tourism and creative economy, a Rahman concert or a run of Bollywood productions shooting on location would be a powerful signal that the region is being repositioned around culture and hospitality rather than conflict.

The momentum has been building: earlier this year, a floating cinema began screening Bollywood classics on Srinagar’s Dal Lake, another sign of the Valley’s cultural revival. For the diaspora, Kashmir remains one of the most emotionally resonant destinations in the subcontinent — a place many second-generation families know only through stories. A Bollywood revival in the Valley, scored and championed by figures like Rahman, gives that longing a contemporary soundtrack.

What comes next

Rahman said talks on a Kashmir performance are ongoing. The International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir, meanwhile, will be the near-term test of whether the Valley can draw the international filmmaking community — and whether Bollywood follows its biggest composer’s advice to point its cameras at the mountains rather than the past.
